n: A bold declaration of faith: if the Lord is my light, my rescue, and my fortress, what is left to fear? Light pushes back darkness, and God pushes back fear.

f.g: Hebrew maʿoz — a stronghold or fortress.

n: Enemies came at David like wild beasts ready to devour him, but they tripped and fell instead. God turned the attack back on the attackers.

f.g: A vivid image of enemies acting like predators eager to destroy.

n: Even if an entire army camped around him, David would stay confident. His courage rests on God, not on the odds.
Above everything, David wants one thing: to live near God, to gaze on his beauty, and to seek him in his house. Many Latter-day Saints love this verse as an expression of devotion to the temple.

f.g: To seek God’s guidance, or to meditate and reflect in his sanctuary.

n: In trouble, God hides his people like a king sheltering a guest in his tent. Then he sets them high on a rock where enemies can’t reach.

f.g: A booth or shelter; a covering place.

n: With his head lifted in victory, David offers joyful sacrifices and songs. His deliverance becomes worship.

f.g: Literally “sacrifices of shouting” — offerings accompanied by glad cries.

n: The mood shifts from confidence to pleading. Faith doesn’t mean never needing to cry out for help.
God had invited, “Seek my face,” and David’s heart answered, “I will.” Seeking God’s face means seeking his presence and closeness.
David asks God not to turn away from him. He recalls that God has helped him before, and pleads with him to keep doing so.

f.g: To hide one’s face is to withdraw favor or presence.

n: Even if the closest human bonds fail — father and mother — God will gather him up. The Lord’s care is deeper than any earthly family’s.

f.g: Gather me in, receive me — as one takes in an abandoned child.

n: Surrounded by people watching for him to stumble, David asks for a clear, level path. Enemies make guidance all the more urgent.

f.g: A level, smooth road without stumbling-blocks.

n: False accusers are breathing out threats of violence. David asks not to be handed over to their wishes.
David would have collapsed if he hadn’t believed he would see God’s goodness in this life. Hope for good in “the land of the living” keeps him going.

f.g: The words “I had fainted” are added by the KJV translators; the Hebrew breaks off, as if too much to say.

n: David turns to counsel his own heart and the listener: wait on the Lord, take courage, and he will give you strength. The repeated “wait” frames the whole promise.
